title: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
summary: Build probability and statistics from counting outcomes: conditioning, Bayes' rule, expectation and variance, the law of large numbers and CLT, maximum likelihood, and confidence intervals and p-values in an A/B test.
outcomes: Compute conditional probabilities and check independence by counting outcomes
Apply Bayes' rule and explain why base rates dominate rare-event predictions
Compute means, variances and standard errors, and explain the 1/sqrt(n) scaling
Explain why minimizing cross-entropy is maximum likelihood estimation
Compute a confidence interval and z-test for an A/B test and interpret its p-value correctly

lessons.title: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does

blocks.md: Machine learning is full of uncertainty: a label may be noisy, a click may or may not happen, a model outputs a *distribution* over next tokens. Probability is the bookkeeping for that uncertainty, and statistics is how you learn its numbers from data. This course builds both from scratch, with one small running example per lesson.

Start with the simplest model of chance: roll two fair six-sided dice. The **sample space** is the set of all possible outcomes, here the 36 ordered pairs (first die, second die). An **event** is a subset of outcomes, such as "the sum is 7". When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is just counting:

- $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{outcomes in } A}{\text{total outcomes}}$

Every probability lies between 0 and 1, the whole sample space has probability 1, and probabilities of non-overlapping events add.

blocks.title: Two dice: 36 equally likely outcomes, colored by their sum

scenes.caption: Each cell is one outcome; the number is the sum of the two dice. All 36 cells are equally likely, each with probability 1/36.
Event A: sum is 7. Six cells lie on the anti-diagonal, so P(A) = 6/36 = 1/6, about 0.167. No other sum has as many cells.
Event B: sum is at least 10. Also six cells (10, 11, 12), so P(B) = 6/36 = 1/6 as well.
Now condition on C: the first die shows 6. The other 30 outcomes are ruled out, so the new sample space is one row of 6 cells. Three of them have sum at least 10, so P(B | C) = 3/6 = 0.5.
Same row, event A instead. Only one of the 6 cells sums to 7, so P(A | C) = 1/6, exactly the unconditional P(A). Learning C changed B's probability but not A's.

blocks.md: **Conditional probability** $P(A \mid C)$ is the probability of $A$ once you know $C$ happened. Knowing $C$ shrinks the sample space to $C$, so you count $A$ only inside it. The general rule, which works even when outcomes are not equally likely, is the ratio below.

blocks.tex: P(A \mid C) = \frac{P(A \cap C)}{P(C)}, \qquad P(A \cap C) = P(A \mid C)\,P(C)
blocks.caption: Definition of conditional probability (for P(C) > 0) and the multiplication rule it implies.

blocks.md: Check it on the figure: $P(B \cap C) = 3/36$ and $P(C) = 6/36$, so $P(B \mid C) = 3/6$. Two events are **independent** when knowing one does not change the other: $P(A \mid C) = P(A)$, which is the same as $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$. The two dice themselves are independent, which is why each cell has probability $\frac16 \times \frac16 = \frac1{36}$.

blocks.prompt: Is "sum is 7" independent of "first die is 6"? Is "sum is at least 10" independent of it?
blocks.reveal:
**Sum is 7: yes, independent.** $P(A \cap C) = 1/36 = (1/6)(1/6) = P(A)P(C)$. Whatever the first die shows, exactly one value of the second die makes 7.

**Sum at least 10: no.** $P(B \cap C) = 3/36 = 0.083$, but $P(B)P(C) = 1/36 = 0.028$. A high first die makes a high sum more likely. Independence is a numeric fact about probabilities, not an intuition about whether events "feel related".

blocks.md: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events ("sum is 2" and "sum is 12") cannot both happen, so learning one happened tells you the other did not: they are strongly *dependent*. Independence means the joint probability factorizes, $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$.
Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

blocks.question: A model's training set has 1,000 emails: 300 are spam, and 240 of the spam emails contain the word "free". Of the 700 non-spam emails, 70 contain "free". What is P(spam | contains "free")?
options: 0.80, because 240 of 300 spam emails contain free
0.24, because 240 of 1,000 emails are spam with free
About 0.77, because 240 of the 310 emails containing free are spam
0.30, the base rate of spam
blocks.explain: Condition on the event you observed: restrict to the 240 + 70 = 310 emails containing "free", of which 240 are spam, so 240/310 = 0.774. Option A is P(free | spam), the reverse conditional, a very common mix-up that the next lesson is about.

blocks.question: You flip a fair coin twice. Let A = "first flip is heads" and B = "the two flips match". Are A and B independent?
options: No, because B depends on the first flip
Yes: P(A and B) = 1/4 = P(A) P(B)
No, because A and B can both happen
It cannot be determined without more data
blocks.explain: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 2/4 = 1/2 (HH or TT), and P(A and B) = P(HH) = 1/4 = P(A)P(B). Even though B is defined using the first flip, it is independent of A. Independence is checked with numbers, not by whether one event is mentioned in the other's definition.

lessons.title: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong

blocks.md: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test catches 90% of sick people (its **sensitivity**, $P(+ \mid \text{sick})$) and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people (its **false positive rate**, $P(+ \mid \text{healthy})$). Your test comes back positive. How likely is it that you are sick?

blocks.prompt: Guess before reading on: is P(sick | positive) closer to 90%, 50%, or 10%?
blocks.reveal: **About 9%.** Most people guess near 90% because they read the sensitivity $P(+ \mid \text{sick})$ as if it were $P(\text{sick} \mid +)$. Those are different conditionals, and the gap between them is set by the **base rate**: how common the disease is to begin with.

scenes.caption: Picture 10,000 people. The base rate splits them first: 1% sick gives 100 sick and 9,900 healthy.
Of the 100 sick, the test catches 90% (90 true positives) and misses 10.
Of the 9,900 healthy, 9% still test positive: 891 false positives. A small rate applied to a huge group gives a big count.
A positive result puts you among 90 + 891 = 981 positives, only 90 of whom are sick: 90 / 981 = 9.2%. The false positives outnumber the true ones about 10 to 1.

blocks.md: **Bayes' rule** is the same calculation in symbols. It flips a conditional you know, $P(E \mid H)$ (evidence given hypothesis), into the one you want, $P(H \mid E)$. It follows in one line from the multiplication rule of the previous lesson, since $P(H \cap E)$ can be written both ways. The denominator $P(E)$ sums over every way the evidence can arise: here, sick and positive plus healthy and positive.

blocks.caption: Prior P(sick) = 0.01, likelihoods 0.9 and 0.09, posterior about 0.092.

blocks.md: The vocabulary carries over to all of ML. The **prior** $P(H)$ is what you believed before the evidence. The **likelihood** $P(E \mid H)$ says how well each hypothesis predicts the evidence. The **posterior** $P(H \mid E)$ is the updated belief. Drag the prior below and watch how strongly the answer depends on it.

blocks.title: Posterior after one positive test, as the base rate changes

scenes.caption: With sensitivity 0.9 and false positive rate 0.09, the same positive test means 1.0% at a 0.1% base rate, 9.2% at 1%, 52.6% at 10% and 90.9% at 50%.
Cut the false positive rate to 0.01 and the 1% case jumps to about 48%. For rare conditions, false positives matter far more than sensitivity.
Back at 0.09 but sensitivity raised to 0.99: the 1% case only moves to about 10%. Catching more sick people barely helps when the healthy group is 99 times larger.

blocks.md: Evidence also stacks. After the first positive, your belief is 9.2%; use that as the prior for a second test. If tests are **conditionally independent** given disease status (an assumption: repeating the same flawed test usually is not), each positive multiplies the **odds** of being sick, $P(\text{sick}) / P(\text{healthy})$, by the **likelihood ratio** $0.9 / 0.09 = 10$.

blocks.title: Belief in sick after repeated positive tests

scenes.caption: Before testing, the belief is the base rate: 1%.
One positive: 9.2%. Still more likely healthy than sick.
A second, independent positive: 50.3%. The posterior from step one became the prior for step two.
A third: 91.0%. Each test multiplied the odds by 10, from 1:99 to about 10:1.

blocks.md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML as a classifier with high recall on a rare class still producing mostly false alarms. Precision is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$ and depends on the base rate; recall is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$ and does not.
Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Strong evidence can be overwhelmed by a small prior, and the denominator just rescales so the posteriors sum to 1.

blocks.question: A fraud model flags 95% of fraudulent transactions and 2% of legitimate ones. Fraud is 0.1% of transactions. Roughly what fraction of flagged transactions are fraud?
options: About 95%
About 50%
About 4.5%
About 0.1%
blocks.explain: Per 100,000 transactions: 100 fraud, 95 flagged; 99,900 legitimate, 1,998 flagged. 95 / (95 + 1,998) = 0.045. The flagging rate on fraud (95%) is recall, not precision; the tiny base rate makes most flags false alarms.

blocks.question: Which change most increases P(sick | positive) for a disease with a 1% base rate, starting from sensitivity 0.9 and false positive rate 0.09?
options: Raise sensitivity to 0.99
Lower the false positive rate to 0.01
Both help equally
Neither, the base rate fixes the answer
blocks.explain: Raising sensitivity takes the posterior from 9.2% to about 10%. Lowering the false positive rate to 0.01 takes it to about 48%, because false positives come from the 99% healthy group and dominate the positives.

lessons.title: Random variables, expected value and variance

blocks.md: A **random variable** is a number attached to each outcome: the value of a die, the number of clicks out of 8 impressions, a model's loss on a random training example. Its **distribution** lists the probability of each value. For a discrete variable this is the **probability mass function** (PMF), $P(X = k)$, and the values sum to 1.

Two numbers summarize a distribution. The **expected value** (mean) $E[X]$ is the probability-weighted average of its values: where the distribution balances. The **variance** $\text{Var}(X)$ is the expected squared distance from the mean: how spread out it is. The **standard deviation** $\sigma$ is the square root of the variance, in the same units as $X$.

One fair die: $E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5$, a value the die never shows, which is fine since it is an average. $\text{Var}(X) = 35/12 \approx 2.92$ and $\sigma \approx 1.71$.

A **Bernoulli** variable is 1 with probability $p$ and 0 otherwise (a click, a correct prediction). Its mean is $p$ and its variance is $p(1-p)$, largest at $p = 0.5$.

Add up $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) trials and you get a **binomial** variable: the number of successes, with $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$. The binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ counts the ways to choose which $k$ of the $n$ trials succeed.

blocks.title: Binomial PMF: number of clicks in n = 8 impressions

scenes.caption: Click probability p = 0.3. The most likely count is 2, and the mean is np = 2.4 with variance np(1 - p) = 1.68.
p = 0.5: symmetric around the mean of 4, variance 2.0. This is the widest of the three because p(1 - p) peaks at p = 0.5.
p = 0.8: mean 6.4, variance 1.28. The mass piles up against the maximum of 8, so the shape skews left.

blocks.md: Two rules make expectations easy to compute. **Linearity of expectation**: $E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]$ for any random variables, independent or not. That is why the binomial mean is just $n$ copies of $p$. **Variances add for independent variables**: $\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)$ when $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and $\text{Var}(aX) = a^2\,\text{Var}(X)$.

blocks.prompt: You roll two dice and add them. What are the mean and variance of the sum? What if you instead roll one die and double it?
blocks.reveal:
Two dice: mean $3.5 + 3.5 = 7$, variance $35/12 + 35/12 \approx 5.83$.

One die doubled: the mean is still 7, but the variance is $2^2 \times 35/12 \approx 11.67$, twice as large. The two independent dice partly cancel each other's luck; doubling one die copies its luck. This is the seed of why averaging many independent samples reduces noise (next lesson).

blocks.md: Continuous variables (a latency, a weight) use a **probability density function** $f(x)$ instead: probabilities are areas under it, $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, and a density value itself can exceed 1. The most important one is the **normal** (Gaussian) distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

blocks.caption: Normal density. About 68.3% of the mass is within 1 sigma of the mean, 95.4% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.

blocks.md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$, where the **covariance** measures how they move together.

blocks.question: An LLM eval has 200 independent questions and the model answers each correctly with probability 0.7. What are the mean and standard deviation of the number correct?
options: Mean 140, standard deviation 42
Mean 140, standard deviation about 6.5
Mean 0.7, standard deviation 0.21
Mean 140, standard deviation 0.46
blocks.explain: Binomial with n = 200, p = 0.7: mean np = 140, variance np(1 - p) = 42, so the standard deviation is the square root, about 6.48. Option A forgets the square root. Runs of the same eval can differ by several questions from noise alone.

blocks.question: X is a die roll and Y = 7 - X (the face on the opposite side). What is Var(X + Y)?
options: Undefined, because X and Y are dependent
blocks.explain: X + Y = 7 always, a constant, so its variance is 0. Adding the variances (35/6) would be wrong because X and Y are perfectly negatively correlated, and the covariance term cancels them exactly. Linearity still gives E[X + Y] = 7.

lessons.title: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT

blocks.md: Everything in statistics rests on one fact: the average of many independent samples is far more predictable than any single sample. Mini-batch gradients, eval accuracies and A/B test conversion rates are all averages, so this lesson explains how much you can trust each of them.

scenes.caption: Twelve rolls of a fair die (generated with a seeded random number generator). The true mean is 3.5.
Early on, each new roll moves the average a lot: a 1 after four rolls pulls it from 3.75 to 3.2.
After 12 rolls the average is 3.08. A 13th roll would shift it by less than 0.25, because it would be 1 of 13. With thousands of rolls it would settle very close to 3.5.

blocks.md: The **law of large numbers** (LLN) says that the sample mean $\bar X_n = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ of independent, identically distributed (**i.i.d.**) samples converges to the true mean $\mu$ as $n$ grows. How fast? Use the rules from the last lesson: the variance of a sum of $n$ independent copies is $n\sigma^2$, and dividing by $n$ divides the variance by $n^2$.

blocks.caption: The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of the sample mean. It shrinks with the square root of n.

blocks.prompt: Your eval accuracy has a standard error of 2 percentage points on 500 questions. How many questions do you need to cut that to 1 point?
blocks.reveal: **2,000 questions, not 1,000.** The standard error scales as $1/\sqrt n$, so halving it needs 4 times the data. Every extra digit of precision costs 100 times more samples.

blocks.md: The **central limit theorem** (CLT) says more: for i.i.d. samples with finite variance, the *shape* of the distribution of $\bar X_n$ approaches a normal curve with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt n$, whatever the shape of a single sample. Watch it happen to a very non-normal variable: a click that happens with probability $p = 0.25$.

blocks.title: Distribution of the observed click rate in n impressions (p = 0.25)

scenes.caption: n = 1: the observed rate is 0 (probability 0.75) or 1 (probability 0.25). Two spikes, nothing like a bell. Exact binomial probabilities, grouped into bins that include their lower edge (a rate of 0.3 counts in 0.3-0.4).
n = 10: already a single hump around 0.25, though still lopsided. Only 28% of runs land in the 0.2 to 0.3 bin. Standard error 0.137.
n = 40: narrower and more symmetric, 53% of runs in the 0.2 to 0.3 bin. Standard error 0.068, half of the n = 10 value because n is 4 times larger.
n = 160: 86% of runs in the 0.2 to 0.3 bin, standard error 0.034. The LLN concentrates the rate around 0.25; the CLT gives the bell shape around it.

blocks.title: Normal approximation to the sample proportion

scenes.caption: n = 10, p = 0.25: SE = 0.137, so the normal curve puts 95% of observed rates within about 0.27 of p; the exact binomial puts 98% there. The approximation is rough at this n, and the curve even leaks below 0.
n = 40: the curve is twice as tall and half as wide.
n = 160: SE = 0.034. The band between the lines holds 95% of the mass: p plus or minus 1.96 SE.
n = 400: SE = 0.022. Try moving p toward 0.5 to see the spread grow, since p(1 - p) is largest there.

blocks.md: The CLT needs independent samples and a finite variance. Correlated samples (consecutive tokens, users who appear many times) have a larger true standard error than $\sigma/\sqrt n$. Very heavy-tailed data converges slowly, and for distributions like the Cauchy, which has no mean, the average never settles at all.

Noise in an average shrinks as $1/\sqrt n$. That single scaling law explains why larger batches give smoother gradients, why small evals are noisy, and why A/B tests need large samples to detect small effects.

blocks.question: Batch size 64 gives a gradient-estimate standard deviation of s (per coordinate, i.i.d. examples). Approximately what does batch size 256 give?
options: s, since batch size does not affect noise
blocks.explain: The mini-batch gradient is an average of per-example gradients, so its standard deviation scales as 1/sqrt(batch). Four times the batch gives sqrt(4) = 2 times less noise, so s/2. The variance falls by 4.

blocks.question: Which statement does the central limit theorem actually support?
options: With enough data, the individual data points become normally distributed
The sample mean of many i.i.d. finite-variance samples is approximately normal
Any average is normal, even of strongly correlated samples
Large samples remove bias from a skewed sampling method
blocks.explain: The CLT is about the distribution of the average (or sum), not the raw data: individual clicks are still 0 or 1. It needs independence and finite variance, and it says nothing about bias: a biased sample averages tightly around the wrong value.

lessons.title: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood

blocks.md: So far the parameters were known: a fair die, a 25% click rate. Statistics runs the other way: you see data and want the parameter. An **estimator** is a rule that turns a sample into a guess, such as the sample mean for $\mu$. Two properties matter. **Bias** is how far its average guess is from the truth; **variance** is how much the guess jumps between samples. The sample mean is unbiased, with variance $\sigma^2/n$ from the last lesson.

**Maximum likelihood estimation** (MLE) is the general recipe. Write the probability of the observed data as a function of the parameter, called the **likelihood** $L(\theta)$, and pick the $\theta$ that makes the data most probable. Example: a coin gives 7 heads in 10 i.i.d. flips. Under heads-probability $p$, that specific sequence has probability $p^7(1-p)^3$.

blocks.tex: L(p) = p^{7}(1-p)^{3}, \qquad \log L(p) = 7\log p + 3\log(1-p), \qquad \frac{d}{dp}\log L = \frac{7}{p} - \frac{3}{1-p} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \hat p = 0.7
blocks.caption: Taking the log turns the product over samples into a sum and does not move the maximum.

blocks.title: Likelihood of p, scaled so the peak is 1

scenes.caption: 7 heads in 10 flips: the peak is at 0.7. A fair coin (p = 0.5) still has 44% of the peak likelihood, so the data barely rule it out.
70 heads in 100 flips: same peak at 0.7, but now p = 0.5 has only 0.03% of the peak likelihood and p = 0.6 has 11.5%. More data sharpens the likelihood.
200 flips: sharper still. The width shrinks roughly as 1 over sqrt(n), the same scaling as the standard error.

blocks.md: This is where most ML loss functions come from. For a classifier that outputs $\hat y_i = P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i)$, the negative log-likelihood of the labels is the **binary cross-entropy**. Minimizing cross-entropy *is* maximum likelihood; with softmax outputs (a probability for each of several classes, summing to 1) it generalizes to categorical cross-entropy, and a Gaussian likelihood with fixed variance gives mean squared error.

blocks.caption: Average negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli labels: binary cross-entropy. For the 7-of-10 coin with p = 0.7 it is 0.611; with p = 0.5 it is log 2 = 0.693.

blocks.md: MLE is not always unbiased. The MLE of a normal variance divides the sum of squared deviations by $n$, which underestimates on average because the deviations are measured from the sample mean, which sits closer to the data than the true mean does. Dividing by $n - 1$ (**Bessel's correction**) removes that bias.

blocks.title: Sample mean and the two variance estimators
blocks.code:
data = [2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 7.0]
n = len(data)
mean = sum(data) / n
ss = 0.0
for x in data:
    ss += (x - mean) ** 2
var_mle = ss / n
var_unbiased = ss / (n - 1)
print(round(mean, 2), round(var_mle, 2), round(var_unbiased, 2))

scenes.caption: Five measurements. The sample mean is 22 / 5 = 4.4.
Sum the squared deviations from the sample mean: 5.76 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.36 + 6.76 = 13.2.
Divide by n for the MLE (2.64) or by n - 1 for the unbiased estimate (3.3). With 5 points the gap is 25%; it vanishes as n grows.

blocks.md: In NumPy, `np.var(x)` divides by $n$ by default (`ddof=0`), while `np.var(x, ddof=1)` divides by $n-1$. pandas `Series.var()` defaults to $n-1$. Check which one a library uses before comparing numbers.

A maximum likelihood estimate from little data can be extreme: 3 heads in 3 flips gives $\hat p = 1$, claiming tails is impossible. Priors (Bayes' rule again), smoothing such as adding pseudo-counts, and regularization all pull estimates away from such overconfident values.

blocks.question: A language model assigns probability 0.5 to every correct next token in a validation set. What is its average cross-entropy (natural log), and what does minimizing it on training data correspond to?
options: 0.5; minimizing the error rate
About 0.693; maximizing the likelihood of the training tokens
About 0.693; minimizing the variance of the predictions
1.0; maximizing accuracy
blocks.explain: Cross-entropy averages -log of the probability given to the correct token: -ln 0.5 = 0.693. Minimizing average negative log-likelihood over the training data is exactly maximum likelihood estimation of the model's parameters.

blocks.question: You compute the variance of 4 validation losses with np.var and compare it to a colleague's number computed with pandas on the same 4 values. Theirs is larger. Why?
options: pandas divides by n - 1 = 3, NumPy by n = 4, so theirs is 4/3 as large
pandas uses the population mean instead of the sample mean
NumPy squares the standard deviation twice
One of you has a bug, since variance is uniquely defined
blocks.explain: np.var defaults to ddof=0 (divide by n) and pandas Series.var defaults to ddof=1 (divide by n - 1). With 4 values the ratio is 4/3. Neither uses a population mean; both subtract the sample mean.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test

blocks.md: A product team tests a new ranking model. Variant A (old) gets 200 clicks from 2,000 users, a 10.0% rate. Variant B (new) gets 240 clicks from 2,000 users, 12.0%. Is B really better, or could a 2 point gap appear by chance? The previous lessons give everything needed to answer.

A **95% confidence interval** is a range built by a procedure that, over many repeated experiments, captures the true value 95% of the time. By the CLT, an estimate $\hat\theta$ with standard error SE is roughly normal, and 95% of a normal lies within 1.96 standard deviations, so the interval is $\hat\theta \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$. For A alone, $\text{SE} = \sqrt{0.1 \times 0.9 / 2000} = 0.0067$, giving 8.7% to 11.3%.

blocks.tex: \text{SE}(\hat p_B - \hat p_A) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p_A(1-\hat p_A)}{n_A} + \frac{\hat p_B(1-\hat p_B)}{n_B}} = 0.0099, \qquad 0.020 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0099 = [0.0006,\ 0.0394]
blocks.caption: Variances of independent estimates add, so the SE of a difference combines both groups. The interval for B minus A barely excludes 0.

blocks.md: A **hypothesis test** asks the same question differently. Assume the **null hypothesis** $H_0$: both variants share one true rate. Pooling all users gives $\hat p = 440/4000 = 0.11$ and a standard error under $H_0$ of $\sqrt{0.11 \times 0.89 \times (1/2000 + 1/2000)} = 0.0099$. The **z statistic** is the observed difference in standard errors: $z = 0.02 / 0.0099 = 2.02$.

blocks.title: Where the observed z falls under the null hypothesis

scenes.caption: If there were no real difference, z would follow this curve. Only 5% of the area lies beyond plus or minus 1.96.
Observed z = 2.02, just past 1.96. The two-sided p-value, the area beyond plus or minus 2.02, is 0.043.
Same 10% vs 12% rates with 8,000 users per arm: z = 4.04, p = 0.00005. The effect did not change, only the sample size; the 95% interval narrows to 1.0 to 3.0 points.

blocks.md: The **p-value** is the probability, computed assuming $H_0$ and the model are true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. Here $p = 0.043$, below the common threshold $\alpha = 0.05$, so the result is called statistically significant. $\alpha$ is the false positive rate you accept: when $H_0$ is true, a 0.05 threshold rejects it 5% of the time.

The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement lists the usual misreadings. A p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true (that is the Bayes' rule mix-up from lesson 2), it does **not** measure the size or importance of an effect, and decisions should not rest only on whether it crosses 0.05. Report the effect size and its confidence interval.

blocks.prompt: You test 20 different model tweaks, none of which actually helps, each at alpha = 0.05 with independent data. How likely is it that at least one looks significant?
blocks.reveal: $1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.64$. **Better than even odds of a false discovery.** Testing many variants, metrics or user segments, or checking a running test repeatedly and stopping at the first significant peek, inflates false positives the same way. Corrections such as Bonferroni (use $\alpha / k$ for $k$ tests) or pre-registering one primary metric control this.

blocks.title: Chance of at least one false positive across k null tests

scenes.caption: One test at alpha = 0.05: a 5% false positive rate, as designed.
Independent tests compound: 1 - 0.95^k gives 22.6% for 5 tests, 40.1% for 10, 64.2% for 20 and 92.3% for 50.

blocks.md: The $\pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$ interval for a proportion (the Wald interval) behaves poorly with small counts or rates near 0 or 1. The NIST handbook recommends the Wilson interval instead.

Every test in this lesson is the same move: estimate, compute its standard error from the variance rules and the CLT, and ask how many standard errors the estimate sits from the null. Significance depends on sample size as much as on effect size.

blocks.question: An A/B test reports p = 0.03 for a lift in click rate. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the new variant is not better
There is a 97% chance the lift is real
If there were no true difference, a gap this large or larger would occur about 3% of the time
The lift is large enough to matter for the business
blocks.explain: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true: it is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data). Getting the probability that the variant is better needs a prior and Bayes' rule. And p says nothing about whether the effect size matters.

blocks.question: Two experiments find the same 0.2 point lift in conversion. Experiment 1 (50,000 users) has p = 0.01; experiment 2 (5,000 users) has p = 0.40. What is the best conclusion?
options: Experiment 2 shows the lift is absent
The experiments contradict each other
Both are consistent with the same lift; experiment 2 is too small to distinguish it from noise
Experiment 1 must have a bug, since the lifts match but p differs
blocks.explain: Same effect, ten times fewer users means a standard error about sqrt(10) = 3.2 times larger, so a much smaller z and larger p. A non-significant result is not evidence of no effect; its confidence interval is just wide enough to include 0.
